title: DSM-106 Full Course Recap
kicker: DSM-106 Business Research · full course recap · S1–S9 (Srinath)
legend: the method and its raw output: the experiment, the stated price, the loading, the DICTION score, the distance, the multiple
the interpretation and the business decision drawn from it: the price move, the construct, the HR intervention, the buy/sell call
footer: Full-course recap for DSM-106 Business Research, S1–S9 (Prof. Jagannathan Srinath). Built from the lecture notes in lectures/. Every number on this page is copied from the notes. The derived arithmetic was rechecked by hand and is consistent with the lecture figures: value per sign-up, the 100-customer pricing scenarios, the distance ratio, CAPM/WACC, ROC, EV/EBITDA re-pricing and the DCF terminal value. The widgets replay the lecture's own cases: Basecamp pricing, the 30-manager attrition dataset, the causal-map comparison and the UK healthcare case, the laptop conjoint, and the Whole Foods Market valuation.
course_notes: Central contrast: amber = the method and what it mechanically outputs (A/B conversion, raw Van Westendorp curves, factor loadings, DICTION scores, z-scores, cognitive distance, multiples, DCF price). Teal = the interpretation and the business decision. The instructor repeats that what matters is 'not the decision per se but the research techniques' (S2) and that 'what is important is how we interpret the results', not the software (S3; R is not mandatory). The second running theme is triangulation: never rely on one method. Combine experiment + survey + scenarios (Basecamp), and survey + text + clustering (attrition). Instructor: Prof. Jagannathan Srinath. Units: USD for Basecamp (per month unless stated) and Whole Foods (USD million unless stated; write 'USD', not the dollar sign, in math-adjacent text). Rupees (₹ crore / lakh) appear only in Indian asides (Adani, Reliance, the company-purchase example, ₹1 crore discounting). DICTION scores, z-scores, cognitive distance (0–1) and conjoint utils are unitless. Exam/assessment statements in the notes: none give an exam format. S2: techniques matter more than the decision. S3: interpretation is assessed, not coding. S9: the final class (S10, not yet recorded) will explain all evaluation components; a group assignment (conjoint survey, or EBITDA-multiple analysis e.g. Adani Enterprises) is proposed but not finalised. Never name students: the notes name many volunteers; write 'a student' and call the two causal-map respondents 'Person A' and 'Person B'. Case names: 'Basecamp', 'Whole Foods Market (WFM)', 'Health Change UK' (voluntary-sector NHS contractor), laptop brand 'Ethos'. The Morieux talk is 'As work gets more complex, 6 rules to simplify'.

modules.plan:
Module 'Basecamp: experiment + survey + scenarios' (S1–S2). Content type: numerical + case.

Cheat cards:
- The business decision (price that maximises CLV) and the founder's four constraints: no price cuts because price signals quality; no feature changes; 'don't be afraid to be ambitious' (club tiers); no historical data.
- Tier table: $29 / $79 / $3,000 per year = $250 per month; free tier = 1 project; pricing not indexed to users or projects.
- A/B test = field (live) experiment vs lab experiment: random assignment, control vs test (2× prices), 1-week conversion window, debrief and charge only the normal price.
- Formula: value per sign-up = conversion rate × average plan value.
- The 'should have doubled' benchmark ($42.25 → $84.50) and the double penalty: volume falls and the mix shifts to the cheapest tier.
- Limitations of the A/B test: cannot be repeated (grievances, 50 staff for millions of users) and it says nothing about +10% … +90%.
- Van Westendorp PSM: the four exact questions (too cheap / bargain / expensive / too expensive) on a $0–$500 slider. Curves and colours: red, orange/yellow, blue, green. Intersections: OPP = red × green; IPP = orange × blue; highest acceptable = orange × green; plus the lowest acceptable price.
- Anchoring bias definition: current users never say they would pay more, so the raw PSM says 'no increase' ($29 tier max $30; $79 tier max $70).
- The fix: re-plot as multiples of the current price (1x) with medians, quartiles and whiskers. Median = 'average consumer' in the instructor's usage.
- The four IQR readings with their medians.
- Decision rule: there is no room to raise price if green sits near 1x and blue sits where yellow is now.
- What Basecamp did: killed Tier 1 and Tier 3 (~1% of customers; conflicts with high-volume, no-customisation); $79 → $99 (+25%, deliberately conservative vs blue median 1.5x); 10% annual prepay discount ≈ $90 per month (lock-in, cash up front).
- Triangulation: the experiment rules out 2×, the survey shows headroom, scenarios size the move. 'Evidence-based decisions still contain guesswork.'

Notes / analogies (cite sessions):
- Founders refuse even $100,000 for a custom build because it would turn a product company into a consulting firm. Jeff Bezos is the only (minority) outside investor; profitability over valuation; no IPO (S1).
- 'Historical data anchors you to what has already happened' (S1).
- A student's Pareto/ABC idea is legitimate and widely practised, but blocked by the constraints (needs a price cut and history): 'as an employee you work within the stated constraints, whatever you think of the founder's rationality' (S1).
- Raising the $29 hero plan by 10–20% is 'guesswork; the optimum could be 50% or 75%' (S1).
- Programme-fee analogy: if MSDSM students were surveyed on a fee rise they would call the current fee too high, and their green median would be about 1.1–1.2x, not 2x. Basecamp's 2x is what signals real headroom (S1, S2).
- Repeated caveat: Basecamp's answer was logically justifiable, not necessarily optimal (S2).
- 'What is important is not the decision per se but the research techniques' (S2).
- Pooling all tiers in one IQR graph is fine because anchoring affects every user the same way; separate $29 and $79 graphs give the same conclusion (S2).

ONE widget: 'Pricing scenario simulator' (the S2 class assignment of 8–10 scenarios).
- Inputs: tier mix fixed at 66 : 33 : 1 out of 100 customers; new single price (slider $79–$200, toggle '10% annual discount', with the class rounding $99 → $90 in the preset); % of the $29 cohort converting (0–100); % of the $79 cohort staying (0–100); enterprise customer kept or dropped (default dropped).
- Readouts: status-quo revenue $4,771; new revenue; change in $ and %; the price jump expressed as a multiple of each cohort's old price (e.g. 29 → 90 = 3.1x).
- Show the jump on a strip with the class IQR landmarks: blue median 1.5x, blue whisker ~3.5x, green median 2x, green Q3 3x, green whisker ~5.3x.
- Verdict: teal if revenue > 4,771, amber if not, plus a note when the jump for the ex-$29 cohort falls in the far tail (beyond 3.5x).
- Presets: 'Status quo'; 'What Basecamp did' ($90, 50% of 66 convert, 100% of 33 stay → $5,940, +$1,169); 'Go to 2x' ($150, ~10 of 66 convert, 60% of 33 ≈ 20 stay → $4,500, below $4,771); 'The 10-customer illustration' (10 × $29 vs 5 × $90).

Static figure, not a widget: the four box plots on a 0–6x axis with the medians and whiskers read in class.

Worked problems:
1. A/B table → value per sign-up for both arms, and why $71.14 fails the $84.50 benchmark.
2. The 100-customer status-quo vs post-change revenue.
3. The 2x counter-scenario and why 29 → 150 (5.2x) sits in the minority tail while 29 → 90 (3.1x) does not.
modules.facts: Tiers: $29/mo; $79/mo (S1 once said $59, corrected); $3,000/yr = 3000/12 = $250/mo. Doubled test prices: $59 (S1; note 2×29 = 58), $149 (S1) or $150 (S2), $6,000/yr = $500/mo. A/B test: 3 days, ~5,000 sign-ups (3,438 + 1,573 = 5,011), 1-week window. Conversion 120/3,438 = 3.49%; 28/1,573 = 1.78%. Average plan value $42.25 vs $71.14. Value per sign-up: 0.0349 × 42.25 = 1.4745 ≈ $1.47; 0.0178 × 71.14 = 1.2663 ≈ $1.27. Benchmark 2 × 42.25 = 84.50; actual rise 71.14/42.25 = 1.684 (+68%; notes say '~60–70%'). PSM slider $0–$500. $29 tier: lowest ≈ $20, OPP ≈ $20, highest ≈ $30 → max increase $1. $79 tier: OPP ≈ $45, IPP ≈ $52.50, highest ≈ $70. IQR in multiples of current price: too cheap median 0.33x (= 66% discount), whisker ~0.9x (S2) / top quartile to 0.8x (S1), outliers 1.2–1.5x. Cheap median 0.67x (S2; ~0.7x S1), Q3 ≈ 1x, whisker ≈ 1.8x, outliers 2, 2.5, 3, 4x. Expensive median 1.4–1.5x, Q3 ≈ 2x, whisker ≈ 3.5x. Too expensive median 2x, Q3 3x, whisker ≈ 5.3x, minority 6x. Programme-fee analogy: green median ~1.1–1.2x. Actual move: 99/79 = 1.253 (+25%). With the 10% annual discount: 99 × 0.9 = 89.10, used as $90 in class. Effective rise 90/79 = 1.139 (notes: '10–14%'). Tier 3 ≈ 1% of customers; revenue claimed up ~20%. 10-customer case: 10 × 29 = 290; 5 × 90 = 450. Break-even share at $90 = 290/90 = 3.22 of 10 ≈ 32%; the lecture said 'even 30% is fine', but 3 × 90 = 270 < 290, so 30% is just below break-even. 100-customer status quo: 66 × 29 = 1,914; 33 × 79 = 2,607; 1 × 250 = 250; total 4,771. Post-change: (0.5 × 66 + 33) × 90 = 66 × 90 = 5,940; gain 5,940 − 4,771 = 1,169 = +24.5%. 2x scenario: 0.6 × 33 = 19.8 ≈ 20; ~10 of 66 convert; 30 × 150 = 4,500; change 4,500 − 4,771 = −271 (−5.7%). Jumps: 90/29 = 3.10x; 150/29 = 5.17x; 150/79 = 1.90x. Scale conflict: S1 ~15 million users, ~7,000 new per week, ~50 employees, Tier 3 storage 2 TB; S2 >1 million customers, 5,000–6,000 per week, Tier 3 storage 1 TB. Tier 1/2 storage 100 GB. S7 recap: PSM ~700–800 responses.

modules.plan:
Module 'From seven survey items to two constructs' (S2 end, S3; recapped in S4). Content type: numerical interpretation + framework.

Cheat cards:
- The dataset: 30 middle managers; items I1–I7 on a 1–10 scale, rated by supervisors and peers monthly and averaged over a year. Give the full item wording.
- First move after any survey: how many groups, and what does each measure.
- Factor analysis = PCA for this course.
- 'If there is difference, there is information; variance = SD².'
- Proportion and cumulative proportion of variance. Rule of thumb: stop once cumulative > 90%.
- Scree plot elbow (here after component 3) vs the 90% rule (2 components): the instructor accepts 2.
- Biplot: vector bundles I1, I4, I5, I6 point right; I2, I3, I7 point top-left; managers appear as points.
- Loadings: RC1/RC2 = rotated components; use magnitude only. Rule: |loading| > 0.5 → belongs (some use 0.6 or 0.7).
- Full chain: components → variance → scree → biplot → loadings → assign → name → composite → compare.
- Factor analysis gives groups, not names.
- Composites: Performance = (I1+I4+I5+I6)/4; ITQ = (I2+I3+I7)/3. Simple average chosen over loading-weighted. 7 items → 2 parameters (dimension reduction).
- Intention precedes behaviour; the lag from intention to quit to actually quitting is ≈ 6 months (6–12).
- Organisational commitment = the literature's 'loyalty'.
- 2×2 intervention matrix: Performance × ITQ.
- Row offset: employee n sits on row n+1.

Notes / analogies (cite sessions):
- I2 (praising another firm's culture) is a leading indicator of attrition; 'an indicator need not be positive, only worth measuring' (S2).
- Competing student groupings (correlational 2 groups, content-based 2 groups, a 3-group leadership/innovation/behaviour scheme) are legitimate hypotheses that need a statistical referee (S3).
- Software policy: R is not mandatory; interpretation is what counts, and any software gives the same result (S3).
- The I3 formality debate: middle managers are the coordinating link and must keep informal trust and reciprocity. Becoming formal = withdrawing → 'silent (quiet) quitting'; 'withdrawal from an organisation begins with withdrawal of informal participation' (S3).
- Morieux talk (S3):
  - Krugman: 'productivity is not everything, but in the long run it is almost everything.'
  - Productivity growth decline: 5% → 3% → 2% → <1%.
  - Holy Trinity: clarity, measurement, accountability.
  - The 4×100 m relay: the US team was 3.2 m ahead on personal bests (6.4 m on that year's bests) yet lost to France. 'Those who carry the baton are slower, but their baton is faster.' 'This is not poetry, this is math.'
  - Clarity: the baton gets dropped at 97 m.
  - Accountability: 'designed to fail in a compliant way'.
  - Measurement: energy goes to the legs, not the arm and the throat.
  - 'It takes to be stupid to cooperate.'
  - Teams waste 40–80% of their time.
  - Go for fuzziness and overlaps; look at the 'how'.
- The instructor's addition: blaming personalities 'adds injustice to ineffectiveness' (S3).

ONE widget: 'Where do you stop?'
- Bars of cumulative proportion of variance for 1, 2, 3, 4 and 7 components. Components 5–6 are greyed: '≈100, not read out'.
- A threshold slider (80%–99%, default 90%) highlights the number of components needed. A fixed marker shows the scree elbow after component 3.
- Readout: components retained, % of information lost.
- Verdict: at 90% → 2 groups (Performance, Intention to Quit), which matches the loadings table. Raising the bar to 95% → 3. The elbow → 3. The instructor accepted 2 because component 3 adds only 4.7%.

Static table, no widget: the item → factor assignment (I2 loading 0.9 is the only loading quoted) and the six candidate factor-label pairs.

Worked problems:
1. Read the variance table and justify 2 components.
2. Assign the 7 items with the 0.5 rule and name the factors.
3. Place employee 9 (Performance 10, ITQ 1.43) and employee 27 (6.79, 10) on the 2×2 and choose interventions.
modules.facts: 30 managers, 7 items (I1–I7), 1–10 scale; annual average of monthly ratings. Cumulative variance: 1 component 58.39% (≈58%; loss 100 − 58 = 42%); 2 components ≈93% (58 + ≈35); 3 components ≈98% (+4.7%; notes give ≈98.4, implying component 2 ≈ 35.3); 4 components ≈99.7%; 7 components 100%. Rule-of-thumb stop: >90% → 2 components. Scree elbow after component 3. Loading cut-off 0.5 (stricter: 0.6 / 0.7); I2 loading cited 0.9 (other loadings not read out). Factor 1 Performance = I1, I4, I5, I6; Factor 2 Intention to Quit = I2, I3, I7. Composites: Performance = (I1 + I4 + I5 + I6)/4; ITQ = (I2 + I3 + I7)/3. Employee 9 (sheet row 10): Performance 10, ITQ 1.43. Employee 27 (row 28): Performance 6.79, ITQ 10. Employee 15 (S4, row 16): 9.28, 10. Observed ranges (S4): Performance 6.78–10, ITQ 1.42–10 (rounding differs from the 6.79 / 1.43 above). Intention → quitting lag ≈ 6 months (6 months to 1 year). Productivity growth: 1950s–early 1970s ~5% p.a.; 1973–83 ~3%; 1983–95 ~2%; since 1995 <1%. Doubling time at 3% = ln2/ln1.03 ≈ 23.4 years (≈ one generation); at 1% = ln2/ln1.01 ≈ 69.7 years (≈ three generations). Relay: 8 finalist teams; US ahead by 3.2 m (summed personal bests) or 6.4 m (that year's bests) but lost to France; '3.5 billion women on earth'. Time wasted: 40%–80%.

modules.plan:
Module 'Text analysis, z-scores and cluster analysis: the attrition pipeline' (S4–S5). Content type: framework + case. ZERO widgets: decision tables and cards carry this module.

Cheat cards:
- Content analysis (DICTION or R): Standard Analysis → report → Compare Viewer. Scores are standardised as if the text were 500 words.
- The five master variables, each with what it measures, its research application and its dark side:
  - Activity: creativity/innovation. Normal range 46.74–55.48. Application: AACSB mission statements → placements, career progress, alumni leaders.
  - Optimism: range 46.37–52.25. Dark side: hubris. Application: CEO utterances in a quarter → negative next-quarter ROI/ROA.
  - Certainty: willpower. Dark side: rigidity. Application: change management via emails and grapevine.
  - Realism: concrete, present, practical. Application: L&D post-training feedback.
  - Commonality: team player. Application: top-management-team transcripts.
- Activity formula: (Aggression + Accomplishment + Communication + Motion) − (Cognitive Terms + Passivity + Embellishment), with why each term is subtracted.
- Operationalisation table: creativity = Activity, team player = Commonality, plus the two survey composites.
- z = (x − x̄)/s and the −3…+3 reading table. Small-sample rule (n = 30): only the sign matters.
- ITQ sign warning: positive z = wants to LEAVE.
- Factor analysis groups variables; cluster analysis groups cases.
- k-means: the analyst picks k from the elbow plot (k = 6); 6 clusters of 5.
- Typology building blocks:
  - Champion = high performance + high creativity; Inert = low on both.
  - Resonant = stays; Dissonant = leaves.
  - Embedded = good team player; Disembedded = poor team player.
- The six-category table and the HR intervention for each (decision table, the module centrepiece):
  - Resonant Embedded Champions: should never leave; if they do, the culture is declining.
  - Dissonant Embedded Champions: failure to 'enchant'; actively retain.
  - Resonant Disembedded Champions: act like a community; accept and acknowledge them.
  - Dissonant Disembedded Champions: embrace the eccentricity.
  - Resonant Inerts: training to 'cognitively transform' performance, else the firm asks them to leave.
  - Dissonant Inerts: peer support, or let go.
- Mixed-methods takeaway: factor + text + cluster analysis together give richer insight than any one technique.

Notes / analogies (cite sessions):
- Employee 15's 47-word appraisal ('strategic mind', 'enterprising', but 'dissent adds to dissonance') → creative, very poor team player, performs, leaving (S4).
- 'People are complicated': employee 6 (Performance 10, Activity 41.92, staying) vs employee 15 (S4).
- Employees 7 and 11 are top performers who want to leave: retain them, maybe pay their MSDSM fees (S4).
- Trump speeches score ~65 on Optimism (S4).
- Cluster 1: 'let them leave', with the joke about warning the MSDSM admissions office (S4).
- ISRO: a champion leaves only if the culture is declining. Google: once a 'dream company', now laying off, so even its resonant embedded champions may go (S5).
- A student's 2-cluster correlation side-analysis: high performers tend to be creative team players, but ITQ is unrelated; 'correlation does not imply causation'. KNN vs k-means mix-up corrected (S5).
- The DICTION version discrepancy for employee 7 (S4).

Static figure: the S5 2-D cluster map.
- Left → right: team play, creativity and performance all rise. Bottom → top: ITQ falls.
- Cluster 1 (24–28) bottom-left = Dissonant Inerts. Cluster 3 (2, 5, 7, 11, 12) bottom-right = Dissonant Embedded Champions. Cluster 5 (1, 3, 8, 9, 10) top = Resonant Embedded Champions.

Worked problems:
1. Read the six-row cluster-means sign table and name each cluster.
2. Compare employees 9 and 11 from the R assignment sheet and prescribe interventions.
3. Judge employee 15's Activity 49.61 and Commonality 16.98 against the ranges.
modules.facts: DICTION normal ranges: Activity 46.74–55.48 (midpoint (46.74 + 55.48)/2 = 51.11; so employee 15's 49.61, called 'slightly on the higher side', is actually below the midpoint); Optimism 46.37–52.25; Trump ≈ 65. Text standardised to 500 words; employee 15 text ≈ 47 words. Employee 15: Activity 49.61, Commonality 16.98, Performance 9.28, ITQ 10. Employee 6: Activity 41.92 (below 46.74), Commonality 44.98, Performance 10, ITQ not read out (wants to stay). Employee 7: Commonality 51.68 (updated DICTION version), Performance 10, ITQ 10. Employee 11: Activity 48.97, Commonality 59.76 (the transcript attributes these to employee 7; context says 11), Performance 10, ITQ 10. Commonality range ≈ 16–78, mean 44.77, SD not read out. Employee 6: 44.98 − 44.77 = +0.21, so by the sign rule her z is slightly positive, though the lecture called her a poor team player. Activity range ≈ 35–61; Performance 6.78–10; ITQ 1.42–10. z = (x − x̄)/s; reading −3 … +3; n = 30 → sign only. k = 6 from the elbow plot; 6 × 5 = 30 employees. Cluster 1 = 24, 25, 26, 27, 28 (Dissonant Inerts); cluster 3 = 2, 5, 7, 11, 12 (Dissonant Embedded Champions; ITQ z ≈ 0.96); cluster 5 = 1, 3, 8, 9, 10 (Resonant Embedded Champions). Employee 1 → cluster 5; employee 9 → cluster 5; employee 11 → cluster 3. S5 group table: 1 low/low/low/leave; 2 low team, above-average creativity, good performance, leave; 3 all good, leave; 4 low/low, good performance, stay (routine-task performers); 5 good/average-good/average-good, stay (ideal); 6 below-average/low-average/low, stay (problem group). S5 itself warns the visual's numbering does not line up perfectly with these group descriptions.

modules.plan:
Module 'Causal maps, cognitive distance and MDS' (S5–S7). Content type: numerical + case.

Cheat cards:
- When to use: a small-sample method (≤ ~20 people: TMT, board, ~10 key clients). It is the middle path between a survey (too little autonomy) and an interview (too much discretion). It is also an intervention methodology.
- Pipeline: interviews with 5–10 people → ≥50 issues → each respondent picks ~10 → draws signed arrows → matrix → compare → insight and action.
- Arrow weights −3 … +3; no arrow = 0; unchosen issue = 100 (placeholder, could be NA).
- Matrix a_ij = impact of row issue i on column issue j. Maps are directional and asymmetric (9→11 = −2 but 11→9 = −3); reciprocal arrows can have opposite signs (20→33 = +1, 33→20 = −1).
- Maps are subjective opinion, not objective truth.
- Recoding rules:
  1. Take |a − b|.
  2. A 100 that pairs with 'not chosen' or 0 → 0.
  3. Residuals 97–103 (one person chose and rated, the other did not choose) → 1.
  4. Genuine differences are kept.
- Distance ratio formula with denominator 6p_c² + 2p_c(p_uA + p_uB) + p_uA² + p_uB² − (6p_c + p_uA + p_uB).
- Bands: 0–0.15 groupthink; 0.16–0.40 functional (ideal); 0.41–0.70 threshold (acceptable, risky); 0.71–1.0 dysfunctional. Both extremes are bad. The group value is the average of the pairwise distances.
- MDS turns the distance matrix (not a correlation matrix) into a map.
- In-direction ID_j = Σ |incoming weights| (signs ignored), summed over the 12 maps. Rank points = 11 − rank. ID beats rank points when they conflict.
- Gap rule: big gaps between successive ranked issues = clarity; small even gaps = confusion.
- Change happens within hierarchical levels first, then across levels; expect 10–20% reductions over ~18 months.
- Course-wide 'which method when' table (S7): large data → experiment, PSM + IQR, factor, text, cluster; small groups → causal maps. List the 10 methods covered.

Notes / analogies (cite sessions):
- Single-map walkthrough (S5): 5→3 +3, 30→3 +3, 30→47 +2, 20→33 +1, 33→20 −1, 5→20 −2 ('not −3, because without leadership competitors can still overtake you'). The slide matrix omitted a(5,20) = −2: spot the error.
- The emailed Excel had a denominator error; corrected to 48 (S6).
- Mumbai Indians: Hardik Pandya returns as captain; Rohit Sharma, Suryakumar Yadav and Jasprit Bumrah are unhappy; camps form; '11 individuals'; near the bottom of the table. High cognitive distance → poor performance (S6).
- 'Gang war': two factions split by a horizontal line in the Phase 1 MDS (S6, S7).
- Health Change UK context: after Labour lost power in 2010, the NHS moved to price-based competitive tendering.
- The four top managers' pre-intervention focuses (competition / government policy / staff motivation / innovation) explain their four MDS corners. After 18 months all four talk competition and pricing. TM01's turnover figures: Service A 55%, Service B 21%, Service C 6% (S6).
- 'Cognitive distance does not fall in a day'; a 10–15% reduction already makes a group manageable. Other uses: sports teams, family counselling (S7).

ONE widget: 'Distance ratio calculator + band gauge'.
- Panel A, 'cell recoder': enter A's and B's value for one cell (each −3…+3, 0, or 100 = not chosen). It shows the raw |difference| and the recoded value, naming which rule fired. Preset cells from the lecture: 10→12 (A 0, B −3 → 3); |100 − 3| = 97 → 1; |100 − (−3)| = 103 → 1; 5→8 → 100 recoded to 0.
- Panel B: sliders for the numerator Σ (0–60) and for p_c, p_uA, p_uB (0–10). It shows each denominator term, then D, with a 0–1 gauge coloured by the four bands.
- Preset 'Person A vs Person B': 18; p_c 2; p_uA 3; p_uB 3 → 24 + 24 + 9 + 9 − 18 = 48 → D = 0.375 → teal 'functional: they would work well together'.
- Markers on the same gauge for the Health Change UK group averages, Phase 1 → Phase 2 (toggle): trustees 0.97 → 0.67; top managers ≈0.856 → 0.69; middle managers ≈0.80 → threshold; all 12 people 0.813 → 0.726 (still just dysfunctional).

Static table: the Phase 1 vs Phase 2 top-issue ID table and the gap computation.

Worked problems:
1. Translate the S5 single map into rows 5, 30 and 47 of the matrix (with the missing −2).
2. Compute the A–B denominator and D, and classify.
3. Interpret the ID gaps 87 − 64 = 23 vs 125 − 60 = 65.
modules.facts: Issue list ≥ 50, choose ~10; classroom demo 15 issues, choose 5; sample ≤ ~20. Weight labels differ between sessions: S5 says +1 moderate, +2 high, +3 very high; S6 says +1 low, +2 moderate, +3 high. Unchosen = 100. Person A chose 7, 9, 10, 11, 12 (empowerment, autonomy, self-confidence, micromanagement, fear of failure). Person B chose 5, 8, 10, 12, 13 (shame, hope, self-confidence, fear of failure, family support). Common {10, 12} → p_c = 2; p_uA = 3; p_uB = 3. A's arrows: 9→11 = −2; 11→7 = −1; 11→9 = −3; 11→10 = +1. Cell 10→12: A 0, B −3 → |0 − (−3)| = 3. Residual examples: |100 − 3| = 97 → 1; |100 − (−3)| = 103 → 1. Numerator 18. Denominator: 6·2² + 2·2·(3 + 3) + 3² + 3² − (6·2 + 3 + 3) = 24 + 24 + 9 + 9 − 18 = 48. D = 18/48 = 0.375 (S6 once said 0.0375: a slip). Bands: 0–0.15 groupthink; 0.16–0.40 functional; 0.41–0.70 threshold; 0.71–1.0 dysfunctional. Health Change UK: 12 people = 2 trustees + 4 top managers + 6 middle managers; 10 of 50 issues; intervention 18 months. Phase 1: trustees 0.97; top managers ≈0.856 (S6, read by a student) / ≈0.85–0.86 (S7), one pair ≈0.675; middle managers ≈0.80; all 12 = 0.813. Phase 2: trustees 0.67; top managers 0.69; middle managers 'into threshold' (no value given); all 12 = 0.726. Overall change 0.813 − 0.726 = 0.087; 0.087/0.813 = 10.7%. MDS camps (Phase 1): top = TR02, TM03, MM03, MM04; bottom = TR01, TM02, TM04, MM01, MM06; middle = TM01, MM02, MM05. ID example: node 3 has 3 incoming arrows, ID = 8 (node 20 has 2 incoming). Rank points = 11 − rank (rank 1 = 10 … rank 10 = 1). ID table: Phase 1 #1 'helping clients achieve recovery' 87, #2 'target focused' 64, #4 'service quality' 43; Phase 2 #1 service quality 125, #2 helping clients achieve recovery 60. modules.plan:
Module 'Conjoint analysis: the Ethos laptop' (S7, second half; data collected at the end of S6). Content type: numerical + procedure.

Cheat cards:
- Research question: which features matter, what each level is worth, and what share the new brand Ethos can win.
- Step 1, design: 7 attributes × levels (brand 6; cores 2; RAM 3; hard drive 3; display size 3; display quality 2; touchscreen 2). Full factorial = product of levels = 1,296, which is infeasible. Computer-generated optimal reduced design = 36 profiles, still covering every level.
- Data: 1–10 ratings (alternatives: 1–5 scale or full ranking). Real studies show pictures or the physical product.
- Respondent fatigue: split the task into batches of 5–6 profiles per sitting.
- Step 2: part-worth utilities (utils) by multiple regression of ratings on attribute levels. Link to diminishing marginal utility.
- Step 3: relative importance (%) summing to 100. Standard formula: range of the attribute's utilities ÷ sum of ranges. This formula was NOT stated in class; mark it 'standard'. 70% rule: take attributes in order of importance until the cumulative total crosses 70%.
- Step 4: market-share simulation. Brand utility can't be changed without advertising, so build the best feature combination for Ethos.
- Include price in real studies to find the launch price point.
- What conjoint delivers: level utilities, attribute importance, share simulation.

Notes / analogies (cite sessions):
- Only 9 of ~28–29 students responded; even 36 profiles caused fatigue (a respondent confirmed it) (S7).
- The counter-intuitive results are the lesson about randomness with n = 9 and tired respondents. Acer is highest; Apple is below locally assembled 'Other', which is 'unlikely in reality'. Dual core is preferred over quad. Normal display is preferred over HD. 4 GB RAM is rated above 16 GB. Hard-drive utilities are all ≈0 (S7).
- 14-inch display preferred (15.2 too bulky, 12 too small): the one result the instructor found plausible (S7).
- The proposed assignment: a new soft drink vs existing ones (e.g. pack size 500 ml / 200 ml), 20–40 responses, at most 5–10 profiles (S7).

ONE widget: 'Design explosion'.
- Steppers for the number of levels of each of the 7 attributes. Preset 'Lecture laptop' = 6, 2, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2.
- An optional 8th attribute, 'Price', with a levels slider (0–5). Label it: not in the lecture design; the lecture said real studies must include price.
- Live readout: the full-factorial product, written out as the multiplication.
- For the lecture preset only, also show: the reduced optimal design = 36 (36/1,296 = 2.8% of the full factorial); sittings needed at 5–6 profiles per sitting (36/6 = 6, 36/5 = 7.2 → 6–8 sittings); and a verdict line comparing 36 with the assignment's 5–10 profile cap.
- Do not compute a 'minimum design' for other configurations (not in the notes).

Static figure: a cumulative bar of the approximate class importances with a 70% line: brand ~40, cores 15–17, RAM ~15, display size 12–13, others <10 each.

Worked problems:
1. Compute the full factorial 1,296.
2. Apply the 70% rule (40 + 15 + 15 ≈ 70, borderline; adding display size crosses it → focus on brand, cores, RAM, display size).
3. Explain why Ethos's simulated ~10% share comes from feature choices, not brand.
modules.facts: Attributes and levels: Brand 6 (Apple, Lenovo, Acer, Asus, Ethos, Other/locally assembled); Cores 2 (dual, quad); RAM 3 (4, 8, 16 GB); Hard drive 3 (256, 512, 1024 GB); Display size 3 (12, 14, 15.2 in); Display quality 2 (normal, HD); Touchscreen 2 (yes, no). Levels vector 6, 2, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2. Full factorial 6 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 2 × 2 = 1,296 (6×2 = 12; ×27 = 324; ×4 = 1,296). Reduced optimal design 36 (first said 18, corrected); 36/1,296 = 2.78%. S6 sheet said 18 combinations, which conflicts with the 36. Ratings 1–10. Respondents 9 (V1–V9) of ~28–29; backup data from 89 people. Batches 5–6 profiles per sitting over 5–6 rounds. Utilities: cores max ≈ 0.5; display quality max ≈ 0.1; hard drive ≈ 0 for all levels; 14 in preferred; 8 GB preferred, 4 GB > 16 GB; Acer highest brand utility; the lowest brand is uncertain (probably Asus); touchscreen preference unclear. Importance ≈: brand 40%, cores 15–17%, RAM 15%, display size 12–13%, others <10% each. Cumulative: 40 + 15 + 15 = 70 (borderline); + 12–13 → 82–85%. Ethos simulated share ≈ 10% (≈ Apple); Acer highest; Other 'good'. Assignment: 20–40 responses, 5–10 profiles. Importance_k = (max u_k − min u_k)/Σ_m (max u_m − min u_m) × 100%: standard formula, not stated in class.

modules.plan:
Module 'Whole Foods: benchmarking, return on capital and cost of capital' (S8). Content type: numerical.

Cheat cards:
- The case dilemma: May 2014; EPS 0.41 expected vs 0.38 actual; dividend raised 0.10 → 0.12; share ≈ USD 48 → 38; Deutsche Bank 'buy up to ~USD 60'.
- Research question: will WFM sustain its premium and profitability?
- Bull vs bear table:
  - Organic segment grows ~20% per year vs grocery 3–4%.
  - WFM's 75 'organic' criteria.
  - Walmart's cheaper organic; Sprouts and The Fresh Market expanding.
  - Doubts on nutrition and water use.
  - Key uncertainty: will consumers care about all 75 criteria?
- Benchmarking: peer groups (organic / mid-level conventional / large retailers); same-store sales growth shows competitors catching up; store counts.
- Formulas:
  - EBITDA margin = EBITDA/Sales.
  - NOPAT = EBIT(1 − t).
  - NWC = CA − CL.
  - Capital = PP&E + NWC.
  - ROC = NOPAT/Capital.
  - EPS = Net income/Shares.
  - CAPM: K_e = r_f + β·MRP.
  - WACC = (D/V)K_d(1 − t) + (E/V)K_e, with V = D + E; the debt term is tax-shielded.
- Credit rating drives K_d (AA 4.29% vs Sprouts BB− 6.83%). Beta drives K_e.
- β intuition: 0.7 moves 0.7% per 1% market move. Standard β = Cov(R_i, R_m)/Var(R_m): supplementary, not given in class; the class intuition σ_company/σ_market is 'not the exact formula'.
- Value rule: ROC > WACC creates value; if WACC > ROC, sell the business.
- Leverage: if K_d < WACC there is room to add debt.
- Caution cards:
  - EBIT/EBITDA were glossed as 'gross profit' in class; standard gross profit = Sales − COGS.
  - MRP was taken as retail growth in class; standard = expected market return − r_f.
  - The instructor's 'long-term loans are cheaper' claim conflicts with a normal upward-sloping yield curve.

Notes / analogies (cite sessions):
- 'A firm can be profitable and raise its dividend yet see its share price fall': the market reads the miss as a weakening competitive position (S8).
- 'Never view net income in isolation; compare it with capital invested, or you might as well put the money in a fixed deposit' (S8).
- 'Borrowing at 15% to earn 13.2% makes no sense' (S8).
- The red line: EBITDA margin ≥ ~9% ↔ ROC ≥ ~13%. Bare minimum ROC > ~7% (just over the 6.9% WACC) (S8).
- BCG: WFM must stay a Star. Its private labels and lower-income-neighbourhood stores largely failed (S8).
- Fixed-income basics: corporate bonds pay interest yearly and repay principal at maturity, like a 15–20-year EMI (S8).
- Indian asides: Adani's ~₹2 lakh crore debt leaves little room to lever; Reliance considered an Aramco stake sale to cut debt-to-value (S8).
- Maturity matching: 30-year r_f with 30-year K_d (S8).

ONE widget: 'Cost of capital vs return on capital'.
- Inputs: r_f (3.4%), MRP (5%), β, K_d, t (39%), D and E (USD million).
- Presets:
  - WFM: β 0.7, D 0, V 14,481 → K_e 6.9%, WACC 6.9%.
  - Walmart: β 0.6, K_d 4.29%, D 55,245, E 251,747 → D/V 0.18, WACC ≈ 5.72%.
  - SuperValu: β 1 → K_e 8.4%. Its D/V 0.57 is shown as a leverage warning; K_d not given, so no WACC.
- Readouts: K_e, after-tax K_d, D/V, WACC.
- A horizontal bar chart compares the chosen WACC with WFM's ROC: FY2011 13.2%, FY2012 ≈14.8%, FY2013 16.3%, 2014F base 17.1%, the 6.3%-margin stress case 9.3%. A dashed red line at 13% (the instructor's ROC red line).
- Verdicts: 'ROC above WACC → creates value'. 'K_d below WACC → room to lever'.

Worked problems:
1. The FY2011 ROC chain: 548 → NOPAT 339 → capital 2,570 → 13.2%.
2. Walmart WACC step by step (and why 0.82, not 0.72, is the equity weight).
3. The EBITDA-margin stress test: 9.4% → ROC ≈ 17.1%, EPS ≈ 1.45 vs 6.3% → ROC ≈ 9.3%, EPS ≈ 0.87, and why the market still punishes it though 9.3% > 6.9%.

modules.plan:
Module 'Valuing Whole Foods: EV/EBITDA multiples and DCF' (S9). Content type: numerical.

Cheat cards:
- EV = market cap + debt; WFM EV = 14,481 with no debt. Leverage: debt adds to firm value.
- EBITDA margin comparison: WFM 9.5%, Walmart 7.5%, Costco 3.8%. Keep the 'EBITDA ≠ gross profit' caution.
- EV/EBITDA multiple. A multiple means nothing alone; compare with peers. Peer choice is a judgment call with no objective benchmark. Size effect: small firms carry high multiples that fall at scale.
- Re-pricing recipe: EV = EBITDA × chosen multiple → ÷ shares (372 million) = price.
- The analyst's 4 steps: compute → judge under/over/fair → choose a multiple → project the price.
- DCF assumptions table: store growth 10.5% / 12.6% / 10% / 3.4%; sales growth 11.1% / 14% / ~12% falling to 8% / 3.4%; EBITDA margin 9.4% / 9.8% / ~9.5% then 9.3%; tax 39%.
- Operating ratios and how to read them by industry:
  - Current asset turnover = Sales/CA (perishables, so high is good; furniture can hold 3–4 months).
  - Current liabilities turnover = COGS/CL with COGS = Sales − EBITDA (WFM pays small organic suppliers fast; Walmart pays late; 'neither is better').
  - Net PP&E per store; D&A per store.
- The 10-step projection.
- NWC can be slightly negative (Walmart).
- ROC = NOPAT/(NWC + Net PP&E) vs cost of capital ~7%.
- FCF = NOPAT − ΔNet PP&E − ΔNWC.
- PV = CF/(1 + r)^t.
- Gordon terminal value TV = FCF/(r − g), discounted by (1 + r)^10.
- EV ÷ shares = share price.
- The scenario table: base USD 58.28 / middle USD 36.13 / worst USD 16.
- What actually happened: margins fell to 6–7%; ROC 17% → 15%; fewer stores; price 48.61 → ~38, rebound to 54.55 (Feb 2015), then down again; Amazon acquired WFM.

Notes / analogies (cite sessions):
- Buying a company: EBITDA ₹200 crore; the seller asks ₹4,000 crore (20×); the buyer says no competitor trades above 10× and offers ₹2,000 crore. 'That is how negotiations work.' A shareholder buys one share, hence per-share prices (S9).
- ₹1 crore next year ≈ ₹93 lakh today (S9).
- Sprouts at 23.6× looks overvalued → a correction is likely (S9).
- The middle case lands on 8.6×, Walmart's multiple. That implies no organic premium at all, so the instructor thinks it may be too pessimistic (S9).
- Indian digression: corporate farming (Reliance Jio, Adani) would allow long credit terms with suppliers, lowering CL turnover and raising profitability, while farmers fear losing land (S9).
- 'Everything depends on the margin projection': it must be an intelligent guess (competitors, customers, competition intensity). Make projections, check them six months later and learn (S9).
- The class's middle case (~USD 36) came closest to reality; Deutsche Bank itself later revised to ~USD 30–35 (S9).

ONE widget (one panel, two modes): 'Re-price Whole Foods'.
- Mode A, 'Multiples':
  - Slider for the EV/EBITDA multiple (4–25) applied to WFM EBITDA 1,222 and 372 million shares.
  - Presets: Walmart 8.6 → USD 28.25; WFM's own 11.9 → ≈ USD 39; Costco 13.6 → ≈ USD 44.7; Sprouts 23.6 → ≈ USD 77.5.
  - Readout: implied EV and price on a price line marked with the market price USD 38.19 and the Deutsche Bank target USD 60.
  - Verdict: below 38.19 → amber 'overvalued at this multiple'; between 38.19 and 60 → 'supports buy'; above 60 → teal 'target justified'.
- Mode B, 'DCF terminal value':
  - Sliders for g (2.0%–4.5%, default 3.4%) and r (6.0%–8.0%, default 7%).
  - The forecast-period PV is held at the base-case 4,328 and the terminal FCF at 1,229. Caption: the 10-year FCF stream is not in the notes, so r only re-prices the terminal value here.
  - Readouts: TV = 1,229/(r − g); PV_TV = TV/(1 + r)^10; EV; price.
  - Base reproduces 34,135 → 17,352 → 21,681 → USD 58.28.
  - Caption: the closer g gets to r, the more the terminal value dominates.
  - The three margin scenarios (58.28 / 36.13 / 16) are shown as a fixed table beside the panel, not recomputed.

Worked problems:
1. Re-price WFM at Walmart's and Costco's multiples.
2. The full base-case DCF arithmetic, from the PV of the forecast period to USD 58.28.
3. Read the scenario table and explain why the margin assumption is the whole story.
modules.facts: Timeline: USD 48.61 (Apr 2014) → USD 38.19 after results; Deutsche Bank target USD 60. EBITDA margins: WFM 9.5%, Walmart 7.5%, Costco 3.8%. WFM EV 14,481 (no debt); EBITDA 1,222; multiple 14,481/1,222 = 11.85 ≈ 11.9. Walmart EV 251,747 + 55,245 = 306,992; multiple 8.6. Costco 13.6. Sprouts 23.6 (EBITDA 187, EV ≈ USD 4.4 bn: 4,400/187 = 23.5). Re-pricing (372 million shares): 1,222 × 8.6 = 10,509 → 10,509/372 = USD 28.25; 1,222 × 13.6 = 16,619 → 16,619/372 = USD 44.68 ≈ 45; 1,222 × 11.85 = 14,481 → 14,481/372 = USD 38.93; 1,222 × 23.6 = 28,839 → USD 77.52. Company-purchase example: 4,000/200 = 20×; 10 × 200 = ₹2,000 crore. Current asset turnover actuals 7.0, 5.6, 6.5 (10,108/1,453 = 6.96); projected 7.2 then 7.6. CL turnover projected 10.5. Net PP&E per store 1,997/311 = 6.42 → USD 6.4 m, labelled 2013 in S9, but S8 used 1,997 as the FY2011 PP&E: conflict. Projected ~USD 5.4 m per store; D&A ~USD 0.89 m per store (~15–16% of PP&E). DCF: g = 3.4%; r = 7% (6.9% rounded); t = 39%. NOPAT example 976 × 0.61 = 595.4 ≈ 596. Discount factors 1/1.07 = 0.9346 (≈ ₹93 lakh per ₹1 crore); 1/1.07² = 0.8734 (lecturer said 0.91–0.92). PV of the forecast period = 4,328. TV = 1,229/(0.07 − 0.034) = 1,229/0.036 = 34,139 (notes 34,135). 1.07^10 = 1.9672; PV_TV = 34,135/1.9672 = 17,352. EV = 4,328 + 17,352 = 21,680 (notes 21,681); price 21,681/372 = USD 58.28. Last actual ROC ≈ 16.37%; projected 20.9% vs cost of capital 6.9–7%. Terminal EBIT ≈ 2,318. Scenarios: base margin ≈ 9.4 → 9.8 → 9.3%, implied multiple 10.8, USD 58.28. Middle: −0.25 pp per year from 9.5%: 9.25, 9.0, 8.75, 8.5, 8.25, 8.0, 7.75, 7.5, 7.25, 7.0, then held at 7.0; multiple 8.6; USD 36.13. Worst: −0.5 pp per year; multiple 8,121/1,679 = 4.84; USD 16. Inconsistencies: 8,121/372 = 21.8 ≠ 16; 1,222 × 10.8/372 = 35.5 ≠ 58.28, so the implied multiples use other spreadsheet cells (flagged unclear in the notes). Do not chain them. Aftermath: ROC 17% → 15%; margins ~6–7%; Feb 2015 USD 54.55; Deutsche Bank later ~USD 30–35; Amazon acquired WFM. Adani Enterprises exercise: share ≈ ₹2,500.
